Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at Example 1 (2024-12-04):
- History starts around 68.02 and gradually moves up to 68.83 on day 18
- Model forecasts are generally lower than true outcomes starting around day 4-5
- The divergence grows over time - by day 25-30, true outcomes are 75-79 while model forecasts are only 66-67

Looking at Example 2 (2024-12-03):
- Very similar pattern - model forecasts are too low compared to true outcomes
- By day 25-30: model forecasts ~67-68, but true outcomes are 74-78

Looking at Example 3 (2024-07-17):
- History around 67-70 range
- Model forecasts are somewhat lower but the divergence isn't as dramatic
- Need to look more closely...

Looking at Example 4 (2024-07-16):
- Nearly identical to Example 3
- Model forecasts are consistently below true outcomes

Looking at Example 5 (2024-07-18):
- Uses history from Example 3 as its basis
- Same pattern of model forecasts being too low

Let me focus on the most striking differences in Example 1 and 2, which show the largest divergence:

In Example 1, looking at the last 10 days of the 30-day forecast vs outcome comparison:
Day 21-30:
Model:    [68.19, 65.66, 65.95, 66.48, 67.50, 66.98, 67.14, 66.83, 67.02]
True:    [74.36, 74.04, 72.17, 73.46, 74.85, 76.92, 76.96, 77.98, 78.33
 
I've identified a critical prediction gap where model forecasts dramatically underestimate true outcomes. The divergence peaks around days 25-30, with true values exceeding model predictions by 6-11 points. This suggests the model lacks sensitivity to emerging market momentum, particularly after sentiment shifts upward.

The consistent underprediction indicates a systematic bias in the forecasting algorithm, especially as the prediction horizon extends beyond 20 days. Sentiment changes seem to amplify this underlying limitation.

I'll need to investigate how sentiment fluctuations interact with these forecast deviations to develop
